questions.prompt: An AE reviews the demo you booked and accepts it against the Demo Qualification Criteria. What is it now?

options.text: An SQL
A meeting held
Closed won
A SAL

questions.prompt: For two weeks you've made 125 dials a day. Connects and conversations look normal, and you're booking more meetings than ever. But SALs went down because AEs rejected several meetings. What's the best place to focus?

options.text: Raise your dials so volume covers the meetings that got rejected.
Rework your opener so more conversations turn into booked meetings.
Check each meeting against the qualification parameters before you book it.
Book meetings closer to the call so fewer of them go cold.

questions.source: Day 1, revenue engine and "120 calls is not the job"

questions.prompt: After the demo, the AE moves the deal to Stage 1, Advanced Talks. What is it now?

options.text: An SQL
A SAL
A host
A booked meeting

questions.prompt: An AE rejects a demo you booked. Which statement best reflects how the role is set up?

options.text: The rejection is the AE's call, so it says little about your own process.
Any booked demo should count, since you own everything through the meeting.
Rejections only start to matter once you're past ramp and on full quota.
The AE decides SAL, so a rejection is a check on the quality of your work.

questions.prompt: It's Wednesday and you have zero meetings this week. Which plan for your 1:1 best fits how we coach?

options.text: Commit to booking two meetings by Friday, whatever it takes.
Ask for a fresh batch of leads, since this list isn't converting.
Audit your dials, prep, conversations and follow-up to find the gap.
Shift time from calls to email until the week turns around.

questions.prompt: What is the daily activity floor for an SDR?

options.text: 120 activities, including at least 100 dials
140 activities, including at least 120 dials
140 dials, with emails and socials on top
100 dials and two booked meetings

questions.prompt: Two reps both make 120 dials a day. Rep A books 8 meetings in a month and 7 become SALs. Rep B books 14 and 6 become SALs. Who had the stronger month?

options.text: Rep B, because more booked meetings means more pipeline created.
Neither, because both reps hit the same daily activity floor.
Rep B, because AE rejections are outside the SDR's control.
Rep A, because more of their meetings survived AE review as SALs.

questions.source: Day 1, "120 calls is not the job" and revenue engine

questions.prompt: What does "host" mean at Momence?

options.text: A current Momence customer
A prospect currently in Attempting status
The AE who runs the demo
Any business inside our TAM

questions.prompt: Which group is made up entirely of Priority 1 verticals?

options.text: Yoga, Pilates, Dance, Spas
Fitness, Wellness, Gyms, Yoga
Yoga, Pilates, Fitness, Wellness
Pilates, Wellness, Spas, Martial Arts

questions.prompt: You have an hour to dial. You have a pre-vetted Pilates list and a pre-vetted dance studio list, both good fits. Where do your dials go first?

options.text: Dance first, since fewer competitors are calling those studios.
Split the hour evenly so you get practice in both verticals.
Pilates only, since dance studios aren't a vertical we book.
Pilates first, since dance is real business but Priority 2.

questions.prompt: What does a class-based business need to clear the activity bar?

options.text: 8+ weekly classes, livestream included
8+ weekly recurring, in-person classes
5+ weekly classes and a waitlist
10+ weekly classes in any format

questions.prompt: A yoga studio lists 10 weekly classes: 6 in person and 4 livestream only. It has a storefront, a working website and an owner on LinkedIn. On class count alone, does it clear the bar?

options.text: No, only the 6 in-person recurring classes count.
Yes, 10 weekly classes is above the 8-class minimum.
Yes, livestream counts as long as it runs every week.
No, studios that livestream are outside our scope.

questions.reveal: It doesn't qualify on class count today. But a storefront, a working website and a findable owner are signs of a real, growing business. Worth a closer look, since they may be adding in-person classes.

questions.prompt: A wellness practice has one bookable practitioner on its widget and books through Acuity. Everything else checks out. Does it qualify?

options.text: Yes, the one-staff exception applies on any booking software.
Yes, wellness is Priority 1, so staff count is waived.
No, one provider only qualifies on an approved platform.
No, appointment businesses need four or more providers.

questions.prompt: A new Pilates studio opens next month. The website is live with a class schedule, but there's no storefront yet. What decides whether you can book?

options.text: Whether they've already chosen booking software
Whether their 8 classes are already running
Whether the owner has run a studio before
Whether a signed lease for the location is known

questions.prompt: A studio owner tells you: "We don't use booking software, and honestly we never want to." What's the right call?

options.text: Qualified, since having no platform today doesn't disqualify them.
Qualified, so book it and let the AE change her mind.
Disqualify, since they explicitly don't want booking software.
Nurture, and check back once the three months are up.

questions.reveal: Before you close it out, find out why. A bad experience with past software is an objection you can work with. A studio that has simply never used it may not know what it's missing.
questions.source: Day 2, "What makes a meeting qualified?"; handbook Software Preference

questions.prompt: Which current software means you don't book the demo?

options.text: Glofox or Arketa
Gymmaster or ClubReady
MindBody or WellnessLiving
Acuity or Vagaro

questions.prompt: While prospecting outbound, you find a studio that clears every check and runs on Mariana Tek. What do you do?

options.text: Work it like any other qualified lead in your Book.
Mark it Unqualified and move on to the next account.
Book it, but only under the one-bookable-staff exception.
Don't pursue it; book only if they say they're unhappy with it.

questions.reveal: Look for clear signs of unhappiness while you pre-vet, like reviews complaining about booking or a post about switching. Without clear signs, leave the account alone.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between ICP and qualified?

options.text: ICP means worth pursuing; qualified means it meets the demo parameters.
ICP means it meets the demo parameters; qualified means the AE accepted it.
ICP covers Priority 1 only; qualified covers Priority 1 and Priority 2.
They're the same check, just done at different points in the process.

questions.prompt: Which list contains only titles a demo can be booked with?

options.text: Owner, Founder, Lead Instructor, Front Desk
Director, Head Coach, Founder, Office Admin
Studio Manager, Instructor, Owner, Bookkeeper
Owner, Founder, Director, Studio Manager

questions.prompt: The person who answers says: "I'm the studio manager. I run the schedule, but the owner makes the call on software." She's interested in seeing Momence. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her to transfer you to the owner before you book anything.
Don't book. She just told you she isn't the decision maker.
Book the demo with her, and ask whether the owner should join it.
Book it, but log it as unqualified until the owner confirms.

questions.source: Day 2, persona slides; handbook Eligible Attendees

questions.prompt: The front desk at a qualified studio says the owner is rarely in and offers to take a message. What's the best outcome to aim for?

options.text: Get the owner's name and the best way and time to reach her.
Give the front desk a short pitch so they can pass it along.
Book the demo with the front desk and add the owner later.
Mark the account Dead, since there's no clear route to the owner.

questions.prompt: An instructor at a qualified studio loves what she hears and wants a demo. The owner hasn't returned your calls. What's the right move?

options.text: Book it with the instructor, since interest is what matters most.
Book it with the instructor and add the owner as an optional guest.
Mark the studio Unqualified, since the owner can't be reached.
Ask the instructor to help you reach the owner or studio manager.

questions.prompt: A studio clears every business check, but there's no named contact anywhere and no qualifying title you can find. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it out of your call list until a named contact turns up.
Call the main line and ask for whoever handles the scheduling software.
Book whoever picks up, then fix the attendee before the demo.
Mark it Dead so nobody else spends time on the account.

questions.prompt: The owner asks her head instructor to take the demo for her. You book it, and the instructor attends alone. Is it likely to become a SAL?

options.text: Yes, because the owner herself asked the instructor to attend.
Yes, as long as the business clears every other qualification check.
Unlikely, because an instructor alone doesn't meet the persona rule.
Only if the instructor is listed as staff on the studio's website.

questions.reveal: If the owner really wants someone else to take the demo, get it in writing or on a recorded call. With that proof, your manager can review the meeting for credit.

questions.prompt: Which are the four business problems Momence is positioned to solve?

options.text: Growth, Pricing, Payments and Billing, Marketing Reach
Growth, Retention, Time and Admin, Client Experience
Retention, Reporting, Staffing and Payroll, Support
Scheduling, Payments, Messaging and Inbox, Reviews

questions.prompt: Which client-side problem do we point to on other platforms?

options.text: Clients can't book a class from their phone without calling the studio.
Booking pages tend to crash during the busiest class times of the week.
Booking can run 8+ steps and forces the client to create an account.
Clients have to confirm every booking by email before it goes through.

questions.prompt: A Pilates studio runs 14 weekly classes and takes every booking through Instagram DMs. Which line works best as the impact?

options.text: "Your clients have to send a DM every time they want to book a class."
"Your clients could book straight from your website in just a couple of clicks."
"Running every booking through DMs is an outdated way to manage a growing studio."
"Someone loses hours sorting DMs, and after-hours requests slip away before they're booked."

questions.prompt: A studio pays separately for scheduling, email marketing and billing, and moves client lists between them. Which value line fits best?

options.text: "Everything lives in one platform, so you stop paying for and syncing four tools."
"Momence has a full marketing suite built right into the same booking platform."
"Momence usually costs less than the booking software your studio pays for now."
"Momence connects to the marketing and billing tools your studio already pays for."

questions.source: Day 2, "They're paying for four tools, not one"

questions.prompt: Which two parts of the pitch change with every prospect?

options.text: Who we help, and the reason to continue
Who we help, and the relevant value
The problem or need, and the relevant value
The reason to continue, and the problem or need

questions.prompt: A rep pitches: "Momence is an all-in-one platform designed to simplify operations for wellness businesses. It has class booking, automated sequences, two-way texting and 24/7 support. Do you have time this week?" What's missing?

options.text: Who we help, stated in a way the prospect recognizes
The prospect's own problem and the one value that fits it
A clear reason to continue to a second conversation
Enough detail on what the product can actually do

questions.source: Day 2, the four-part pitch and "What actually separates them"

questions.prompt: In Problem → Impact → Value, what's true of the value step on a cold call?

options.text: It's the full list of features that could apply.
It's the price difference versus their software.
It's the step you can usually skip to save time.
It's a hypothesis until the prospect confirms it.

questions.reveal: If the prospect isn't biting, don't keep pushing the same value. Ask what's actually costing them time or money, and change the value to match the pain they describe.

questions.prompt: A studio's website shows no schedule, just a contact form. HubSpot says they're on MindBody. What do you build relevance from?

options.text: What's usually true for studios on MindBody, like multi-step booking.
Momence's full feature list, since there's nothing specific to use.
Ask the prospect to walk you through how their business runs.
Hold off calling until you can find something specific to them.

questions.prompt: A teammate writes "it's frustrating for the owner" as the impact. What's the best coaching?

options.text: It works, since emotion is what drives most buying decisions.
Turn it into time, money or a client the business is losing.
Skip ahead to the value, since the impact is already implied.
Replace it with the Momence feature that removes the frustration.

questions.source: Day 2, "You have the problem. Find the rest."

questions.prompt: In what order do you pre-vet a lead?

options.text: Context → business fit → persona fit → decision
Business fit → persona fit → context → decision
Persona fit → business fit → decision → context
Business fit → context → decision → persona fit

questions.prompt: Every lead leaves pre-vetting in one of which four states?

options.text: New, Attempting, Booked, Dead
Attempting, Recycled, Nurture, Booked
New, Nurture, Unqualified, Customer
Attempting, Nurture, Unqualified, Dead

questions.prompt: A studio owner asks you never to contact her again. Which status does the lead get?

options.text: Dead
Nurture
Unqualified
Attempting

questions.prompt: HubSpot lists a lead as Yoga. The website shows a 24-hour gym with open floor space and no class schedule. What do you go with?

options.text: HubSpot, since the vertical was checked when the lead came in.
Neither yet; call and ask which vertical they consider themselves.
The website, which means it's a gym and not a fit for us.
Mark it Nurture until someone confirms the right vertical.

questions.source: Day 2, "So… who should you actually work?"

questions.prompt: You've confirmed fit, found the founder, and noted they're on MindBody. Twelve minutes in, you're curious about their Instagram. What now?

options.text: Write up the note and move on; more won't change your decision.
Keep going, since more context always makes for a better call.
Check their reviews too, in case they reveal a pain point.
Park it and come back when you have time to finish properly.

questions.prompt: A qualified studio's owner says: "Not interested right now. We're in the middle of opening a second location." Where does the lead end up?

options.text: Unqualified, since she told you she isn't interested.
Nurture, since it qualifies but isn't ready for outreach.
Dead, so nobody on the team calls her again by mistake.
Attempting, and try her again tomorrow afternoon.

questions.reveal: Nurture is where it ends up, not your first move. A second location is a reason to talk now: more schedules, more staff, more clients to manage. Make that case first. If she still says no, then Nurture.

questions.prompt: You're pre-vetting a Pilates studio: 11 weekly in-person classes, Founder on LinkedIn, runs on MindBody. A teammate says skip it because they already have software. Who's right?

options.text: Your teammate, since studios on a competitor rarely switch.
Your teammate, unless the studio has posted about switching.
You, since competitor software proves the booking pain exists.
You, but only call if you can reach the founder directly.
